claim: Effective perceptual decisions rely upon combining sensory information with knowledge of the rewards available for different choices.
source: Effective perceptual decisions rely upon combining sensory information with knowledge of the rewards available for different choices.
evidence: This is a general statement about perceptual decision-making that draws from established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: It is not known where reward signals interact with the multiple stages of the perceptual decision-making pathway and by what mechanisms this may occur.
source: However, it is not known where reward signals interact with the multiple stages of the perceptual decision-making pathway and by what mechanisms this may occur.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current scientific knowledge, which is the motivation for the study.

claim: Microstimulation was less effective in shifting perceptual choices towards the stimulus preferences of the stimulated neurons when available reward was larger.
source: Microstimulation was less effective in shifting perceptual choices towards the stimulus preferences of the stimulated neurons when available reward was larger.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: A bounded accumulation decision model revealed that the interaction of expected reward with microstimulation can be explained if expected reward modulates a sensory representation stage of perceptual decision-making, in addition to the better-known effects at the integration stage.
source: A bounded accumulation decision model, applied to analyse behavioural performance, revealed that the interaction of expected reward with microstimulation can be explained if expected reward modulates a sensory representation stage of perceptual decision-making, in addition to the better-known effects at the integration stage.
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting results presented in Table 1 and Figure 5, showing significant effects of reward on parameter k (sensory representation).

claim: When sensory information is used simply to signal the availability of reward in value-based decisions, the activity of lateral intraparietal (LIP) neurons correlates with the relative reward an animal can expect for a particular choice.
source: When sensory information is used simply to signal the availability of reward in value-based decisions, the activity of lateral intraparietal (LIP) neurons correlates with the relative reward an animal can expect for a particular choice (Platt and Glimcher, 1999; Sugrue et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies by Platt and Glimcher (1999) and Sugrue et al. (2004).

claim: Perceptual decision-making has been successfully modelled as a bounded evidence-accumulation process in which sensory evidence about the visual stimulus is represented in sensory cortex and then integrated over time in sensorimotor structures such as lateral intraparietal cortex (area LIP).
source: Perceptual decision-making has been successfully modelled as a bounded evidence-accumulation process in which sensory evidence about the visual stimulus is represented in sensory cortex and then integrated over time in sensorimotor structures such as lateral intraparietal cortex (area LIP) (Shadlen and Newsome, 2001; Roitman and Shadlen, 2002; Mazurek et al., 2003; Huk and Shadlen, 2005; Gold and Shadlen, 2007) (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous modeling studies and is illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Previous human neuroimaging and animal electrophysiology studies found that when perceptual decision-making is modelled in this way, information about reward is reflected only at the integration stage, represented in sensorimotor structures such as area LIP.
source: Previous human neuroimaging and animal electrophysiology studies found that when perceptual decision-making is modelled in this way, information about reward is reflected only at the integration stage, represented in sensorimotor structures such as area LIP (Rorie et al., 2010; Summerfield and Koechlin, 2010; Mulder et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies by Rorie et al. (2010), Summerfield and Koechlin (2010), and Mulder et al. (2012).

claim: Activity of motion- and disparity-selective neurons in visual area V5/MT have been closely linked to animals' subjective perception during discrimination of structure-from-motion (SFM) visual stimuli.
source: On the other hand, activity of motion- and disparity-selective neurons in visual area V5/MT have been closely linked to animals' subjective perception during discrimination of structure-from-motion (SFM) visual stimuli (Dodd et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dodd et al. (2001).

claim: Neurons in primary visual cortex (area V1) can respond to visual sensory signals that do not reach perception.
source: Primary visual cortex (area V1) comprises the initial stage of visual information processing but neurons here can respond to visual sensory signals that do not reach perception (Cumming and Parker, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cumming and Parker (1997).

claim: Microstimulation biases perceptual choices towards visual interpretations that match the tuning of the stimulated neurons.
source: Microstimulation biases perceptual choices towards visual interpretations that match the tuning of the stimulated neurons (Krug et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Krug et al. (2013).

claim: Blood-oxygen level dependent (BOLD) signals in sensory cortex are modulated by reward probability, size and delivery.
source: Blood-oxygen level dependent (BOLD) signals in sensory cortex are modulated by reward probability, size and delivery (Pleger et al., 2008; Serences and Saproo, 2010; Weil et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies by Pleger et al. (2008), Serences and Saproo (2010), and Weil et al. (2010).

claim: The BOLD signal is an indirect measure of neural activity that averages the responses of many neurons, including those that are excited by the sensory stimulus and those that are inhibited by it.
source: However, the BOLD signal is an indirect measure of neural activity that averages the responses of many neurons, including those that are excited by the sensory stimulus and those that are inhibited by it (Logothetis et al., 2001; Logothetis and Wandell, 2004), and may be differentially affected by modulatory signals in comparison to neuronal spiking (Boynton, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Logothetis et al. (2001), Logothetis and Wandell (2004), and Boynton (2011).

claim: V1 activity was predicted by the reward value of a stimulus relative to other stimuli in a saccadic curve-tracing task.
source: This study showed that V1 activity was predicted by the reward value of a stimulus relative to other stimuli, implying that reward signals have the potential to reach the earliest stages of sensory cortical processing (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is based on a study by Stanisor et al. (2013) mentioned in the preceding sentence.

claim: Electrical microstimulation of small populations of neurons in relevant cortical regions, combined with sensory stimulation, can produce reliable changes in perceptual reports, which are specific to the stimulus preferences of the neurons at the microstimulated site.
source: Electrical microstimulation of small populations of neurons in relevant cortical regions, combined with sensory stimulation, can produce reliable changes in perceptual reports, which are specific to the stimulus preferences of the neurons at the microstimulated site (Salzman et al., 1990, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Salzman et al. (1990, 1992).

claim: When the stimulated neurons encode combinations of visual cues, microstimulation adds a signal that is specific to that combination, as found in cortical area V5/MT for visual motion and binocular disparity.
source: When the stimulated neurons encode combinations of visual cues, microstimulation adds a signal that is specific to that combination, as found in cortical area V5/MT for visual motion and binocular disparity (Krug et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Krug et al. (2013).

claim: Electrical microstimulation of area V5/MT biases animals' choices towards the cylinder rotation direction preferred by the multi-unit in 28 out of 48 sites.
source: As previously reported, electrical microstimulation of area V5/MT biases animals' choices towards the cylinder rotation direction preferred (PREF) by the MU (χ2 likelihood-ratio test of nested models Equations 1a,b, p < 0.05 in 28 out of 48 sites; Fle: 13/20 sites; Ica: 15/28 sites) (Krug et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical testing of the experimental data and citation to Krug et al. (2013).

claim: There was a significant interaction between the slope of the fitted psychometric function and available reward size, indicating better performance in large reward trials.
source: There was a significant interaction between the slope of the fitted psychometric function and available reward size, indicating better performance in large reward trials (χ2 likelihood-ratio test of nested models Equations 2a,b, 'Materials and methods': p = 0.001; Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical testing of the data shown in Figure 3.

claim: An increase in either the stimulus sensitivity (parameter k) or the distance between the DV starting point and the bounds (parameter B) can improve performance according to the bounded accumulation model.
source: According to the bounded accumulation model, an increase in either the stimulus sensitivity (represented by parameter k) or the distance between the DV starting point and the bounds (represented by parameter B, Equation 3a, 'Materials and methods'; Figure 4B) can improve performance (Figure 4C; compare to Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is based on model simulations shown in Figure 4C and theoretical understanding of the bounded accumulation model.

claim: If performance in large reward trials improves as a result of an increase in B, this will not affect the size of the microstimulation shift, because B acts at an integration stage that is positioned after the location at which visually evoked and electrically evoked signals have been combined.
source: If performance in large reward trials improves as a result of an increase in B, this will not affect the size of the microstimulation shift, because B acts at an integration stage that is positioned after the location at which visually evoked and electrically evoked signals have been combined (Figure 4E; see also Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is based on model simulations shown in Figure 4E and logical inference from the model structure.

claim: If performance improves as a result of an increase in k, this will decrease the relative influence of microstimulation on perceptual choices because k acts specifically on visually evoked sensory representations before they are combined with electrical microstimulation signals.
source: If performance improves as a result of an increase in k, this will decrease the relative influence of microstimulation on perceptual choices (illustrated by a smaller horizontal shift between microstimulated and non-microstimulated psychometric functions) because k acts specifically on visually evoked sensory representations before they are combined with electrical microstimulation signals (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is based on model simulations shown in Figure 4F and logical inference from the model structure.

claim: The size of the microstimulation effect was decreased in large reward trials compared to small reward trials.
source: The size of the microstimulation effect - the horizontal shift between microstimulated and non-microstimulated psychometric functions—was decreased in large reward trials (dashed lines) compared to small reward trials (smooth lines), implicating a change in stimulus sensitivity (parameter k) by reward (see Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5 and model fitting results.

claim: For both animals, parameter k was significantly increased in large compared to small reward trials.
source: For both animals, parameter k was significantly increased in large compared to small reward trials (χ2 likelihood-ratio test of nested models Equations 3 a,b: Fle: p < 0.001; Ica: p < 0.001; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical testing of model fits, with results shown in Table 1.

claim: The estimated distance between the starting point of DV integration and the decision bounds (parameter B) was significantly affected by reward, decreasing in large compared to small reward trials.
source: The estimated distance between the starting point of DV integration and the decision bounds, represented by parameter B, was also significantly affected by reward, decreasing in large compared to small reward trials (χ2 likelihood-ratio test of nested models Equations 3a,c: Fle: p = 0.007; Ica: p < 0.001; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical testing of model fits, with results shown in Table 1.

claim: Expected reward affects perceptual decision-making both at the sensory representation stage (parameter k) and the integration stage (parameter B).
source: Altogether these results indicate that expected reward affects perceptual decision-making both at the sensory representation stage (parameter k) and the integration stage (parameter B).
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the model fitting results showing significant effects of reward on both parameters k and B.

claim: The normalised microstimulation shift was significantly smaller for large expected reward trials (median = 0.67) compared to small expected reward trials (median = 0.88).
source: The normalised microstimulation shift was significantly smaller for large expected reward trials (median = 0.67) compared to small expected reward trials (median = 0.88; Wilcoxon sign-rank test of normalised shift values, two-sided: n = 28, p < 0.001)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical testing of the data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The raw microstimulation shift was significantly smaller for large expected reward trials (median = 0.0064°) compared to small expected reward trials (median = 0.0093°).
source: Similarly, the raw microstimulation shift was significantly smaller for large expected reward trials (median = 0.0064°) compared to small expected reward trials (median = 0.0093°; Wilcoxon sign-rank tests of raw shift values: n = 28, p < 0.001)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical testing of the data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Performance in the ∆dx control was significantly better in large reward compared to small reward trials.
source: As observed in the electrical microstimulation experiments, there was a significant improvement in performance in trials where a larger reward was available for a correct choice (χ2 likelihood-ratio test of nested models Equations 2a,b: Ica-∆dx: p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical testing of the control experiment data shown in Figure 7.

claim: There was no significant interaction between reward condition and ∆dx-induced shift in the ∆dx psychometric functions.
source: However, there was no significant interaction between reward condition and ∆dx-induced shift in the ∆dx psychometric functions (χ2 likelihood-ratio test of nested models Equations 2a,c: Ica-∆dx: p > 0.05; Figure 7)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical testing of the control experiment data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Both animals' cylinder discrimination thresholds significantly correlated with stimulus eccentricity, worsening as eccentricity increased.
source: Both animals' cylinder discrimination thresholds significantly correlated with stimulus eccentricity, worsening as eccentricity increased (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The raw overall microstimulation effect significantly correlated with the cylinder discrimination threshold at each site.
source: The raw overall microstimulation effect also significantly correlated with the cylinder discrimination threshold at each site (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The reward modulation of the raw microstimulation shift effect was significantly correlated with stimulus eccentricity and with the raw overall microstimulation effect size for both animals considered together, and for one animal considered alone (Ica).
source: The reward modulation of the raw microstimulation shift effect was significantly correlated with stimulus eccentricity and with the raw overall microstimulation effect size for both animals considered together, and for one animal considered alone (Ica), such that the biggest raw effects of reward on microstimulation occurred for sites with largest eccentricity (where thresholds were high) and the biggest raw overall microstimulation effect (Figure 8C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analyses shown in Figure 8C and 8D.

claim: The correlations between reward modulation and eccentricity/microstimulation effect disappeared when microstimulation shift was normalised by cylinder discrimination threshold at each site.
source: However, these correlations disappeared for reward modulation of the microstimulation shift effect when normalised by cylinder discrimination threshold at each site (Figure 8E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analyses shown in Figure 8E and 8F.

claim: The reward effect is constant when microstimulation is expressed as a fraction of the discrimination threshold.
source: This shows that the reward effect is constant when microstimulation is expressed as a fraction of the discrimination threshold.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the disappearance of correlations when data are normalized by threshold (Figure 8E,F).

claim: There was no correlation between normalised reward effect size and the amount of performance fluctuation across microstimulation sites.
source: There is no correlation between normalised reward effect size and the amount of performance fluctuation across microstimulation sites, either for animals separately or together (Pearson's product–moment correlation: p >> 0.05 in all cases), suggesting that performance fluctuation cannot explain the reward effect on microstimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The effect of microstimulation was significantly smaller in large compared to small expected reward trials in both good epochs and bad epochs.
source: For both types of epoch, the effect of microstimulation was significantly smaller in large compared to small expected reward trials (χ2-test of nested models Equations 2a,c: good epochs: p < 0.001; bad epochs: p < 0.001), showing that the effect of expected reward on microstimulation remains present in different states of task engagement.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical testing of data separated by performance epochs, shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: When both choices are associated with larger rewards, the distance to both decision bounds might be expected to decrease.
source: When both choices are associated with larger rewards, as in the present study, the distance to both decision bounds might be expected to decrease, as we, and others (Rorie et al., 2010), have found.
evidence: This claim is based on the current study's findings and citation to Rorie et al. (2010).

claim: A decrease in distance-to-bound would impair performance accuracy when available reward is large because the closer proximity of the DV to the bounds would result in a greater effect of accumulated noise on the final perceptual choice.
source: On its own, this effect would impair performance accuracy when available reward is large because the closer proximity of the DV to the bounds would result in a greater effect of accumulated noise on the final perceptual choice (Bogacz et al., 2006, 2007; Rorie et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is based on theoretical understanding of the bounded accumulation model, supported by citations to Bogacz et al. (2006, 2007) and Rorie et al. (2010).

claim: The reciprocal increase in sensitivity to the visual stimulus balances the decrease in accuracy resulting from the shorter distance-to-bound, so that overall performance improves when available reward is larger.
source: However, the reciprocal increase in sensitivity to the visual stimulus, discussed above, balances the decrease in accuracy resulting from the shorter distance-to-bound, so that overall performance in fact improves when available reward is larger, as we observe.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined effects of changes in parameters k and B observed in the study.

claim: Previous studies found that information about reward was reflected only at the integration stage of visual perceptual decision-making, represented in sensorimotor structures.
source: Previous studies found that information about reward was reflected only at the integration stage of visual perceptual decision-making, represented in sensorimotor structures (Feng et al., 2009; Rorie et al., 2010; Summerfield and Koechlin, 2010; Gao et al., 2011; Mulder et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Activity in sensory cortex can be modulated by reward in tasks such as cued curve-tracing saccade task, somatosensory discrimination, and visual stimulus selection tasks.
source: However, experiments employing other types of task, such as a cued curve-tracing saccade task (Stanisor et al., 2013), somatosensory discrimination (Pleger et al., 2008), tasks in which a subject must select between two presented visual stimuli (Serences, 2008; Serences and Saproo, 2010), or a fixation task where a reward is delivered with or without a visual cue (Arsenault et al., 2013), found that activity in sensory cortex can also be modulated by reward.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: The source of the reward signal affecting sensory cortex may reflect an influence from prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, or amygdala, known to represent reward and value predictions during decision-making.
source: The source of the reward signal affecting sensory cortex may reflect an influence from prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, or amygdala, known to represent reward and value predictions during decision-making (Rushworth and Behrens, 2008; Bermudez and Schultz, 2010; Levy and Glimcher, 2012), or neuromodulation by serotonergic neurons originating from the dorsal raphe nucleus, which also signal reward (Cohen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on known functions of these brain regions cited from previous studies.

claim: Dopaminergic reward-predicting neurons may indirectly modulate or enhance sensory cortical activity.
source: Another significant source of reward signals in the brain are dopaminergic reward-predicting neurons, which may also indirectly modulate or enhance sensory cortical activity (for review, see Schultz 2002).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on a review by Schultz (2002).

claim: Area V5/MT has a specific role in 3D depth processing.
source: Area V5/MT has been shown to have a specific role in 3D depth processing (Dodd et al., 2001; Krug et al., 2004; Krug and Parker, 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Area V5/MT contains specialised intrinsic connectivity suitable for combining visual depth and motion signals.
source: and to contain specialised intrinsic connectivity suitable for combining visual depth and motion signals (Ahmed et al., 2012), relevant for the cylinder stimulus.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ahmed et al. (2012).

claim: The SFM stimulus portrays two transparent surfaces of moving dots, with the dots on one surface moving in the opposite direction from the dots on the other surface, generating a percept of a rotating cylinder with a compelling sensation of 3D depth.
source: This stimulus portrays two transparent surfaces of moving dots, with the dots on one surface moving in the opposite direction from the dots on the other surface. This pattern of motion generates a percept of a rotating cylinder with a compelling sensation of 3D depth (Treue et al., 1991) (Video 1).
evidence: This claim describes the visual stimulus used in the study, supported by citation to Treue et al. (1991) and Video 1.

claim: Adding binocular disparities to the dots defines the depth order of the two dot surfaces and specifies the direction of rotation of the cylinder to be clockwise (CW) or counter-clockwise (CCW) as viewed from above.
source: Adding binocular disparities to the dots defines the depth order of the two dot surfaces and specifies the direction of rotation of the cylinder to be clockwise (CW) or counter-clockwise (CCW) as viewed from above.
evidence: This describes a property of the visual stimulus based on established principles of binocular vision.

claim: If both dot surfaces have zero disparity, then the depth order of the stimulus is ambiguous and the perception is bistable.
source: If both dot surfaces have zero disparity, then the depth order of the stimulus is ambiguous and the perception is bistable (Nawrot and Blake, 1989; Parker and Krug, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nawrot and Blake (1989) and Parker and Krug (2003).

claim: Microstimulation experiments were conducted in one cortical hemisphere in two adult male rhesus macaque monkeys.
source: Microstimulation experiments were conducted in one cortical hemisphere in two adult male rhesus macaque monkeys (Macaca mulatta).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental subjects.

claim: Area V5/MT was identified by established physiological criteria including the approach through grey/white matter pattern, neurons' characteristic direction selectivity and binocular disparity selectivity, the relationship between size and eccentricity of receptive fields, and the relationship between RF positions and known topography.
source: Area V5/MT was identified by established physiological criteria: (1) the approach through the grey/white matter pattern comprising the striate cortex, lunate sulcus and the posterior bank of the superior temporal sulcus (STS) (Zeki, 1974); (2) by neurons' characteristic direction selectivity and binocular disparity selectivity and its clustering in V5/MT (Van Essen et al., 1981; Maunsell and Van Essen, 1983; Albright and Desimone, 1987; Bradley et al., 1995, 1998; DeAngelis et al., 1998; DeAngelis and Newsome, 1999); (3) the known relationship between the size and eccentricity of V5/MT receptive fields (Desimone and Ungerleider, 1986); and (4) from penetration to penetration, the relationship between RF positions and known topography of V5/MT (Albright and Desimone, 1987).
evidence: This claim describes the methods used to identify V5/MT, supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Electrical microstimulation was applied during the 2000 ms of stimulus presentation on half of the trials, pseudo-randomly interleaved with non-microstimulated trials.
source: Electrical microstimulation was applied during the 2000 ms of stimulus presentation on half of the trials, pseudo-randomly interleaved with non-microstimulated trials.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental procedure.

claim: Stimulation consisted of 20 µA biphasic pulses of 200 µs cathodal stimulation followed by 200 µs anodal stimulation, delivered at 200 Hz.
source: Stimulation consisted of 20 µA biphasic pulses of 200 µs cathodal stimulation followed by 200 µs anodal stimulation, delivered at 200 Hz.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the microstimulation parameters.
